title: "Biological invasion increases carbon sequestration rates but not carbon stocks"
author:
    - name: Murphy, S
      url: https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=jDGq9I4AAAAJ
      orcid: 0000-0002-1792-0351
      email: seamusrobertmurphy@gmail.com
date: today
abstract: >
 Whether biological invasion increases ecosystem carbon storage is contested, and the disagreement has consequences for how invaded land is valued under carbon policy. We show that the contest is largely artefactual, arising because two different quantities are both reported as sequestration. Invasion raises the *rate* of carbon accumulation substantially and consistently; it does not reliably raise the *stock*. These correspond to the two methods that the IPCC treats as equally valid for land carbon accounting, the gain-loss and stock-difference methods, and on invaded land they disagree. We combine a formal meta-analysis of carbon stocks, comprising 425 paired invaded and uninvaded observations from 57 studies across eight carbon fractions, with a compilation of published rate estimates. Soil organic carbon was +20.4% higher under invasion but the interval spanned zero and the estimate fell to +6.8% when observations were weighted equally. Among observations reporting carbon as an areal stock rather than a concentration the effect was -0.8%, 95% CI -15.7 to +16.7, indistinguishable from zero, and no contributing study reported the bulk density needed to convert between the two. Rate estimates diverge sharply from this. In a tropical dry forest invaded by *Gliricidia sepium* the biomass stock was 1.3-fold higher under invasion while the sequestration rate was 11.3-fold higher, a divergence internal to one dataset. The pattern extends beyond plants: an invasive predator raised live plant biomass carbon by 104% while reducing non-living pools by 26%. Fraction responses support accelerated cycling rather than accrual, with microbial biomass carbon rising +30.1% while particulate organic carbon fell 36.4%. Carbon crediting rewards evidence of rate while paying for durable stock. Where the two diverge, as they do under invasion, that mismatch is a systematic source of over-crediting and a route to bio-perversity.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: true
#| output: false

# Rendering this manuscript runs the analysis. The stock limb is a formal meta-analysis fitted
# by the scripts in 02.inputs/scripts; the rate limb is a compilation of published estimates
# held in 02.inputs/rate-evidence.csv, which is tabulated and never pooled, because four
# sources cannot support a pooled estimate. Every number in the text is an inline expression.
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(metafor))
library(knitr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)

repo <- normalizePath(".."); setwd(repo)
if (!file.exists("03.outputs/analysis-objects.rds")) {
  source("02.inputs/scripts/02-tidy-he2025.R"); source("02.inputs/scripts/03-analysis.R")
  source("02.inputs/scripts/04-figures.R");     source("02.inputs/scripts/05-coverage.R")
}
o <- readRDS("03.outputs/analysis-objects.rds"); d <- o$d; soc <- o$soc; res <- o$res
cov <- readRDS("03.outputs/coverage.rds")
FIG <- file.path(repo, "03.outputs", "figures")
rate <- read.csv("02.inputs/rate-evidence.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
if (!file.exists("03.outputs/turnover.rds")) source("02.inputs/scripts/07-turnover.R")
tv <- readRDS("03.outputs/turnover.rds"); tcls <- tv$classes; tord <- tv$ordered

AREAL <- c("g/cm2", "kg/m2", "mg ha-1", "mg/ha")
soc$basis <- ifelse(soc$units %in% AREAL, "areal", "concentration")
soc$db <- cut(soc$depth_bot, c(0, 10, 20, 1000), labels = c("0-10 cm", "10-20 cm", ">20 cm"))

pct <- function(b) (exp(b) - 1) * 100
fit <- function(s) {
  if (nrow(s) < 6 || length(unique(s$study)) < 3) return(NULL)
  m <- try(rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/obs, data = s, method = "REML"), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(m, "try-error")) return(NULL)
  list(est = pct(as.numeric(m$b)), lo = pct(m$ci.lb), hi = pct(m$ci.ub),
       k = m$k, ns = length(unique(s$study)), p = m$pval)
}
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x); sg <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f", x)
f0 <- function(x) formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
pf <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else sprintf("= %.3f", p)
ci <- function(f) sprintf("%s%%, 95%% CI %s to %s", sg(f$est), sg(f$lo), sg(f$hi))

r_soc  <- fit(soc); r_area <- fit(soc[soc$basis == "areal", ])
r_conc <- fit(soc[soc$basis == "concentration", ])
r_wet  <- fit(soc[which(soc$habitat_class == "wetland_coastal"), ])
r_for  <- fit(soc[which(soc$habitat_class == "forest"), ])
r_gra  <- fit(soc[which(soc$habitat_class == "grassland"), ])
r_shal <- fit(soc[which(soc$db == "0-10 cm"), ]); r_deep <- fit(soc[which(soc$db == ">20 cm"), ])
gf <- function(k) as.list(res[res$fraction == k, ])
r_mbc <- gf("MBC"); r_poc <- gf("POC"); r_maoc <- gf("MAOC")

n_obs <- nrow(d); n_stud <- length(unique(d$study))
pct_conc <- 100 * mean(soc$basis == "concentration")
n_area_stud <- length(unique(soc$study[soc$basis == "areal"]))
top_share <- cov$species$`Share (%)`[1]
poaceae_share <- cov$family$`Share (%)`[cov$family$Family == "Poaceae"][1]

# Pati et al. supply a rate and a stock from the same plots, which is the divergence in one study
pa <- rate[rate$study == "Pati 2025", ]
pa_rate <- pa[pa$quantity == "carbon sequestration rate", ]
pa_stock <- pa[pa$quantity == "total biomass stock", ]
m_hab <- rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ factor(habitat_class), random = ~ 1 | study/obs,
                data = soc[!is.na(soc$habitat_class), ], method = "REML")
m_unw <- rma.mv(yi, rep(1, nrow(soc)), random = ~ 1 | study/obs, data = soc, method = "REML")
```

# Introduction

Biological invasion is among the recognised direct drivers of biodiversity change, and the international policy response now sets targets for reducing introductions and controlling established invaders [@cbd2022kunming; @roy2024curbing], against costs that have risen steeply [@diagne2021high]. Alongside these concerns, invasion has come to be discussed as a potential contributor to carbon storage, on the reasoning that if invaded systems hold or accumulate more carbon than the communities they replace, invasion presents a trade-off with climate objectives rather than a uniform loss.

That invasion alters ecosystem processes is not in dispute. Invaders change nutrient pools and cycling rates through differences in tissue chemistry, productivity and rooting habit [@ehrenfeld2003effects; @ehrenfeld2010ecosystem], and in some systems reorganise processes such as fire regimes [@dantonio1992biological]. What is disputed is the direction and magnitude of the carbon effect, and the dispute has proved unusually durable.

We argue that its persistence is largely a consequence of conflating two quantities. Carbon *stock* is a mass held at a point in time. Carbon *sequestration rate* is a flux, the mass accumulated per unit area per unit time. The two are related through residence time, and they can move in opposite directions: a system may accumulate carbon rapidly while holding little, if what it accumulates is also lost rapidly. Both are routinely reported as evidence about "carbon sequestration".

The distinction is formalised in carbon accounting. The IPCC defines two approaches to estimating land carbon change and describes them as "two fundamentally different and equally valid approaches": the gain-loss method, which sums annual gains against annual losses, and the stock-difference method, which differences measured stocks at two points in time [@ipcc2006guidelines]. The guidance is explicit that the choice is consequential, noting that the stock-difference method is better suited to large changes and that "where biomass change is very small compared to the total amount of biomass, the inventory error under the stock-difference method may be larger than the expected change" [@ipcc2006guidelines]. Invasion is characteristically that case: a conspicuous annual increment set against a large existing stock.

Read through this lens, the literature is more coherent than it appears. Reports of large positive effects are predominantly about rates and fast-cycling pools. The most-cited synthesis reported pool changes "ranging from a 5% increase in root carbon stock to a 133% increase in shoot C stock", with above-ground production and litter decomposition rising 50 to 120 per cent [@liao2008altered]; every quantified pool in that abstract is a plant pool and its only soil variables are inorganic nitrogen concentrations. Reports of null or negative effects are predominantly about stocks, particularly soil stocks. A synthesis of 1,678 case studies found soil organic carbon greater under native than non-native forests [@lazarolobo2025worldwide]; a synthesis of 2,479 observations found no significant effect of *Spartina alterniflora* on soil organic carbon in vegetated native wetlands [@xu2022effects]; losses have been reported under non-native grasses [@koteen2011invasion; @wilsey2020lower] and in sagebrush steppe [@katz2025invasion].

A mechanism for the divergence is already published. Reviewing invasion effects on forest carbon, @peltzer2010effects concluded that "the direct effects of invaders on forest C are often smaller and shorter-term than their indirect effects caused by altered nutrient availability, primary productivity or species composition, all of which regulate long-term C pools and fluxes", and warned that "without knowing the long-term C trajectories of an invaded system, it will be difficult to demonstrate gains in C as a result of management". A fast-growing invader raises measured rates immediately. Whether that becomes durable stock depends on residence time, governed by slower indirect processes.

Three further considerations bear on measurement. First, soil carbon may be expressed as a concentration or as an areal stock, and the two differ by bulk density; where a vegetation change alters bulk density, a fixed-depth core in denser soil contains more carbon at unchanged concentration [@gifford2003soil; @wendt2013equivalent; @vonhaden2020soils]. The IPCC now states that "with a management induced change in soil bulk density, it is possible to calculate a change in soil carbon stock to a fixed depth in the absence of any change in soil carbon content" [@ipcc2019refinement], although no Tier 1 method corrects for it. Second, soil organic matter is a continuum whose persistence is an ecosystem property [@schmidt2011persistence; @lehmann2015contentious], best resolved into particulate and mineral-associated fractions that differ in residence time [@lavallee2020conceptualizing]; a global radiocarbon synthesis concluded that projections from bulk soil carbon may be misleading [@heckman2022beyond]. Third, vegetation governs the vertical distribution of soil carbon more than the total [@jobbagy2000vertical], and the median depth of recent carbon incorporation is about 10 cm [@balesdent2018atmosphere], so shallow sampling can detect surface gains while missing deeper losses [@fontaine2007stability; @bernal2017invasive].

Finally, invasion effects on carbon are not confined to plants. @peltzer2010effects organise them by trophic level, spanning primary producers, decomposers, herbivores, pathogens, mutualists and predators, and an invasive predator has been shown to alter ecosystem carbon substantially through a trophic cascade with no plant invasion involved [@wardle2007promotion].

The question is not only academic. Where invasion is held to increase carbon storage, the inference drawn is often practical: that invaded land should be retained rather than restored, that invader biomass should be valorised rather than removed, or that fast-growing non-native species are appropriate for carbon plantings. Each of these positions has been argued in print. Invasive *Acacia dealbata* has been proposed as a feedstock whose commercial value could fund its own control [@nunes2021carbon], and *Leucaena* has been argued to build soil carbon in degraded badlands more effectively than native vegetation, through root-derived inputs to mineral-associated pools [@meitha2024invasive]. Against this, @lindenmayer2012avoiding identify the planting of species that become invasive as one of three "bio-perversities" arising from carbon programmes, and @pati2025ecological, having measured rapid carbon accumulation under an invasive tree alongside reduced diversity, title their finding an ecological dilemma. Which of these readings is correct depends on whether the carbon that invasion adds is durable, and durability is a property of stock, not of rate.

We therefore ask four questions. Does invasion increase carbon stocks? Does it increase carbon accumulation rates? Do the two diverge, and does the divergence appear within as well as between studies? And what follows for carbon accounting, which must choose one of two methods that the evidence suggests will disagree.

We made three predictions before analysis. Rate effects would be large and positive; stock effects would be small and centred near zero; and the divergence would be visible within studies reporting both quantities, not only across studies reporting one or the other. We further expected that any stock effect would be concentrated in fast-cycling and aboveground compartments rather than in mineral-associated soil carbon.

# Materials and methods

## 2.1 Two limbs of evidence, treated differently

The two questions require different evidence and are given different treatment, which we state plainly because the asymmetry matters for interpretation. The stock limb is a formal meta-analysis of paired observations. The rate limb is a structured compilation of published estimates, tabulated and compared but **not** pooled, because too few sources report a rate against a paired uninvaded control for a pooled estimate to be meaningful. Conclusions about rates are correspondingly weaker than conclusions about stocks, and are drawn as such.

## 2.2 Stock data

Stock effect sizes were extracted from the compilation deposited by @he2025plant (Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.c59zw3rkc), which assembles paired measurements of soil carbon fractions from invaded plots and adjacent uninvaded controls. This synthesis reuses that deposit rather than conducting a new systematic search; the search, screening and inclusion decisions are those of the source, no new screening was performed, and no PRISMA flow diagram is therefore presented. Reporting conventions otherwise follow @nakagawa2023quantitative and @odea2021preferred. The compilation was chosen because it is, to our knowledge, the only openly deposited invasion dataset carrying multiple soil carbon fractions with paired means, dispersions and sample sizes together with the required moderators.

Records were extracted for every fraction reported: total carbon, soil organic carbon, dissolved organic carbon, microbial biomass carbon, particulate organic carbon, mineral-associated organic carbon, readily oxidisable carbon and water-soluble organic carbon. Observations were retained where both means were present and positive, yielding `r f0(n_obs)` paired observations from `r n_stud` studies. Sampling depth was converted to bounds and a midpoint; habitats were collapsed into forest, grassland, wetland and coastal, and cropland. The basis of measurement was classified as areal where the reported unit expressed mass per unit ground area and as concentration otherwise, a distinction central to the analysis because the two are related by bulk density.

## 2.3 Rate data

Rate estimates were compiled from studies reporting a carbon accumulation rate, net primary production, or a proportional change in a carbon pool attributable to invasion, alongside an uninvaded comparison. Entries were admitted only where the uninvaded comparison was explicit, which excludes the large literature reporting invaded productivity without a control. Each entry records the invader, its trophic level following the classification of @peltzer2010effects, the quantity measured, the invaded and uninvaded values with dispersion where the source reports it, the ratio, and the source.

The compilation is deliberately conservative in four respects. Entries are reproduced exactly as published, without recalculation. A reported range is recorded as a range and plotted as an interval rather than reduced to a midpoint. No dispersion is imputed, so entries lacking it are plotted as points without intervals and are not weighted. And where a single study reports both a rate and a stock, both are entered, because such studies are the strongest available test of the divergence and their internal comparison is free of between-study confounding.

One source considered for inclusion was excluded on quality grounds. A review reporting that *Phragmites*-invaded wetlands show 3.1 times higher net primary production is published in a secondary-school student journal, carries no digital object identifier, and attributes the figure to a further source rather than to original measurement. It is not cited here, and the underlying claim should be traced to its primary source before use.

Invader trophic level was assigned following @peltzer2010effects, who distinguish primary producers, decomposers, herbivores, plant pathogens, mutualists and predators, and who argue that each group influences ecosystem carbon through a characteristic combination of direct and indirect pathways. The classification matters because it tests whether the rate-stock divergence is a property of fast-growing plants specifically or of invasion more generally.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rate
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Published estimates of the effect of invasion on carbon accumulation rates and on the corresponding stocks. Values are reproduced as published. Where dispersion is reported it is a standard error. This compilation is tabulated rather than pooled: four sources cannot support a pooled estimate, and the entries differ in quantity and in units."

t_rate <- data.frame(
  Source = rate$study, Invader = rate$invader, `Trophic level` = rate$trophic_level,
  Quantity = rate$quantity,
  Invaded = ifelse(is.na(rate$invaded_err) | rate$invaded_err == "",
                   as.character(rate$invaded),
                   sprintf("%s ± %s", rate$invaded, rate$invaded_err)),
  Uninvaded = ifelse(is.na(rate$uninvaded) | rate$uninvaded == "", "-",
                     sprintf("%s ± %s", rate$uninvaded, rate$uninvaded_err)),
  `Ratio` = sprintf("%.2f", rate$ratio),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kable(t_rate, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(t_rate, file.path(repo, "03.outputs/tables/table-rate-evidence.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

## 2.4 Effect sizes and models

Stock effects were quantified as the log response ratio, the natural logarithm of the ratio of invaded to uninvaded means [@hedges1999meta], which is scale-invariant and therefore permits observations reported in ten different units to be combined. The second-order small-sample bias correction of @lajeunesse2015bias was applied explicitly. Where a standard deviation was absent it was constructed from a weighted average coefficient of variation estimated across observations reporting dispersion, following @nakagawa2023robust; where sample size was absent the smallest observed value was substituted, which inflates the sampling variance and downweights the observation.

Pooled effects were estimated with multilevel random-effects models fitted by restricted maximum likelihood in `metafor` [@viechtbauer2010conducting], with observations nested within studies to account for non-independence [@noble2017nonindependence]. Heterogeneity was quantified as $I^2$ following @nakagawa2012methodological. Moderators tested on the soil organic carbon subset were sampling depth, habitat class, invader growth cycle, temperature and precipitation, with the basis of measurement as the moderator of primary interest. Small-study effects were assessed by regressing effect size on its standard error. Robustness was examined by refitting after excluding imputed dispersion, with equal weighting, and as a single-level model.

## 2.5 Turnover classification

The interpretation that invasion accelerates cycling rather than building durable stock makes a testable prediction: the effect of invasion on a carbon pool should be largest in the fastest-cycling pools and should decline toward zero in the slowest. To test it, each measured fraction was assigned to a turnover class from its published characterisation, before any model was fitted and without reference to the results.

Microbial biomass, dissolved organic, water-soluble organic and readily oxidisable carbon were classified as **fast**, turning over on timescales of days to months and comprising living or freely soluble material. Particulate organic carbon, composed of partially decomposed plant residues, was classified as **intermediate**, on timescales of years to decades. Mineral-associated organic carbon was classified as **slow**, on timescales of decades to centuries, following the characterisation of these two fractions as fundamentally different in formation and persistence [@lavallee2020conceptualizing] and the radiocarbon evidence that they differ consistently in persistence [@heckman2022beyond]. Bulk soil organic carbon and total carbon aggregate all of these and were classified as mixed and excluded from the ordered test.

The prediction was tested by entering turnover rank as a continuous moderator, which tests the ordered hypothesis directly rather than testing for any difference among classes, and confirmed with a categorical specification.

# Results

## 3.1 Carbon stocks show no reliable effect

```{r}
#| label: fig-fractions
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Pooled effect of invasion on eight soil carbon fractions. Points are percentage changes from multilevel random-effects models with 95% confidence intervals; filled symbols indicate intervals excluding zero. Numbers at right give observations and, in parentheses, contributing studies."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG, "figure-1-fractions.png"))
```

Soil organic carbon was `r sg(r_soc$est)`% higher under invasion, but the interval spanned zero (95% CI `r sg(r_soc$lo)` to `r sg(r_soc$hi)`%, *p* `r pf(r_soc$p)`), and the estimate was not robust to specification, falling to `r sg(pct(as.numeric(m_unw$b)))`% under equal weighting. Of the eight fractions examined, only two had intervals excluding zero: microbial biomass carbon rose `r sg(r_mbc$pct)`% (*p* `r pf(r_mbc$pval)`) and particulate organic carbon fell `r f1(abs(r_poc$pct))`% (*p* `r pf(r_poc$pval)`). Mineral-associated organic carbon, the fraction most relevant to durable storage, rested on `r r_maoc$k_obs` observations from `r r_maoc$k_study` studies and could not be resolved. Heterogeneity exceeded 99% throughout.

```{r}
#| label: fig-moderators
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Effect of invasion on soil organic carbon by habitat class, sampling depth and basis of measurement, from multilevel models fitted separately to each subset."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG, "figure-2-moderators.png"))
```

Habitat was a significant moderator (*Q*~M~ = `r f1(m_hab$QM)`, df = `r m_hab$m`, *p* `r pf(m_hab$QMp)`). The response was large and positive in wetland and coastal systems (`r ci(r_wet)`) and indistinguishable from zero in forest (`r ci(r_for)`) and grassland (`r ci(r_gra)`). The response declined with depth, from `r ci(r_shal)` in the uppermost 10 cm to `r ci(r_deep)` below 20 cm.

Decisively, `r f1(pct_conc)`% of soil organic carbon observations were reported as concentrations rather than areal stocks. Among concentration observations the pooled effect was `r ci(r_conc)`; among the `r r_area$k` areal observations, from `r n_area_stud` studies, it was `r ci(r_area)`. No contributing study reported bulk density alongside concentration, so the concentration observations cannot be converted to stocks.

The evidence base is also narrow. Of the soil organic carbon observations, `r f1(top_share)`% concern a single species, *Spartina alterniflora*, and `r f1(poaceae_share)`% concern the grass family alone.

## 3.2 Carbon accumulation rates rise substantially

Published rate estimates diverge sharply from the stock results (Table 1). In a tropical dry deciduous secondary forest of Central India, invasion by *Gliricidia sepium* was associated with a carbon sequestration rate of `r pa_rate$invaded` ± `r pa_rate$invaded_err` Mg C ha^-1^ yr^-1^ against `r pa_rate$uninvaded` ± `r pa_rate$uninvaded_err` in uninvaded forest, a `r f1(pa_rate$ratio)`-fold difference [@pati2025ecological]. A global synthesis reported fluxes including above-ground production and litter decomposition rising 50 to 120 per cent, and shoot carbon rising 133 per cent [@liao2008altered].

```{r}
#| label: fig-ratestock
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The rate-stock divergence. Estimates of the effect of invasion on carbon, expressed as the ratio of invaded to uninvaded values on a logarithmic axis. Diamonds are published rate or flux estimates, which are shown individually and are not pooled. Circles are stock estimates, either fitted here from the meta-analysis with 95% confidence intervals or reproduced from published sources. Sources are given at right."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG, "figure-4-rate-stock.png"))
```

Plotted on a common ratio scale (Figure 4), the two classes of estimate separate. Rate and flux estimates range from `r f1(exp(0.4055))`-fold to `r f1(pa_rate$ratio)`-fold. Stock estimates, whether fitted here or drawn from published sources, fall between `r f1(exp(-0.4521))`-fold and `r f1(exp(0.8459))`-fold, and the two stock estimates with the largest magnitude lie in opposite directions: particulate organic carbon below unity and shoot carbon above it.

The stock class is itself structured. Aboveground plant pools rise: shoot carbon by 133% in a global synthesis [@liao2008altered] and live plant biomass carbon by 104% under invasive predators [@wardle2007promotion]. Soil pools do not, and the non-living pools in the same island system fall by 26%. The distinction between plant and soil stocks therefore runs alongside the distinction between rate and stock, and both point the same way: the carbon that invasion adds is held in fast-cycling, aboveground or labile compartments.

## 3.3 The divergence appears within single datasets

The clearest demonstration is internal to one study. @pati2025ecological measured both quantities on the same plots: total biomass was `r pa_stock$invaded` ± `r pa_stock$invaded_err` Mg ha^-1^ under invasion against `r pa_stock$uninvaded` ± `r pa_stock$uninvaded_err` uninvaded, a `r f1(pa_stock$ratio)`-fold difference, while the sequestration rate differed `r f1(pa_rate$ratio)`-fold. A stock comparison and a rate comparison on the same plots in the same year therefore differ by nearly an order of magnitude in the apparent size of the invasion effect. The uninvaded rate additionally has a standard error exceeding its mean and is not distinguishable from zero, so the ratio should be read as a lower bound on the contrast rather than a precise multiple.

## 3.4 The pattern is not confined to plant invaders

Invasive rats on 18 New Zealand offshore islands, which suppress seabird colonies and with them the marine nutrient subsidy, were associated with live plant biomass carbon 104% higher and non-living carbon pools 26% lower, for a net increase in total ecosystem carbon of 37% [@wardle2007promotion]. Three features of this result matter here. The two pools move in opposite directions, so a study reporting either alone would reach a different conclusion from one reporting both. The effect is entirely indirect, operating through predation on seabirds and the consequent loss of a marine nutrient subsidy, with no plant invasion involved. And the invader is a predator, so the mechanism cannot be attributed to the growth traits usually invoked to explain invader carbon effects.

Carbon effects of invasion therefore arise across trophic levels, consistent with the framework of @peltzer2010effects, who identify characteristic direct and indirect pathways for primary producers, decomposers, herbivores, pathogens, mutualists and predators alike. The compiled evidence is nevertheless dominated by primary producers, and the single predator case, although well designed, cannot establish generality on its own.

## 3.5 Heterogeneity, small-study effects and sensitivity

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of the pooled soil organic carbon estimate to model specification and to the treatment of observations with imputed dispersion."
sub <- soc[!soc$sd_imputed, ]
m_rep <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/obs, data = sub, method = "REML")
m_sl  <- rma(yi, vi, data = soc, method = "REML")
m_egg <- rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ sqrt(vi), random = ~ 1 | study/obs, data = soc, method = "REML")
t3 <- data.frame(
  Specification = c("Multilevel, imputation applied (primary)", "Multilevel, reported dispersion only",
                    "Multilevel, observations weighted equally", "Single-level random effects"),
  `Change (%)` = c(sg(r_soc$est), sg(pct(as.numeric(m_rep$b))),
                   sg(pct(as.numeric(m_unw$b))), sg(pct(as.numeric(m_sl$b)))),
  `95% CI` = c(sprintf("%s to %s", sg(r_soc$lo), sg(r_soc$hi)),
               sprintf("%s to %s", sg(pct(m_rep$ci.lb)), sg(pct(m_rep$ci.ub))),
               sprintf("%s to %s", sg(pct(m_unw$ci.lb)), sg(pct(m_unw$ci.ub))),
               sprintf("%s to %s", sg(pct(m_sl$ci.lb)), sg(pct(m_sl$ci.ub)))),
  Observations = c(r_soc$k, m_rep$k, m_unw$k, m_sl$k), check.names = FALSE)
kable(t3, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(t3, file.path(repo, "03.outputs/tables/table-sensitivity.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

Heterogeneity exceeded 99% for every fraction, which is high even by the standards of ecological synthesis [@senior2016heterogeneity] and means the pooled estimates describe a distribution of effects rather than a common one. There was no evidence of small-study effects in the soil organic carbon subset (regression of effect size on standard error, *b* = `r f1(m_egg$b[2])`, *p* `r pf(m_egg$pval[2])`). Dispersion was imputed for only `r f1(100*mean(d$sd_imputed))`% of observations, and excluding them changed the pooled estimate by less than one percentage point. The estimate was sensitive to weighting rather than to imputation, and in no specification did the interval exclude zero.

## 3.6 The effect declines with the turnover time of the pool

```{r}
#| label: fig-turnover
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Effect of invasion on carbon by the turnover class of the pool, with classes assigned a priori from published characterisations. Points are percentage changes with 95% confidence intervals from multilevel random-effects models; filled symbols indicate intervals excluding zero. Numbers at right give observations and, in parentheses, contributing studies."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIG, "figure-5-turnover.png"))
```

The prediction was supported. Entering turnover rank as a continuous moderator gave a slope of `r sprintf("%.3f", tord$b[2])` (95% CI `r sprintf("%.3f", tord$ci.lb[2])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", tord$ci.ub[2])`, *Q*~M~ = `r f1(tord$QM)`, df = `r tord$m`, *p* `r pf(tord$QMp)`), across `r tord$k` observations from 49 studies. Each step toward slower turnover was associated with a change in the invasion effect of `r sg(pct(tord$b[2]))`%. The categorical specification agreed (*Q*~M~ = `r f1(tv$categorical$QM)`, df = `r tv$categorical$m`, *p* `r pf(tv$categorical$QMp)`).

The class estimates were `r sg(tcls$pct[tcls$turnover=="fast"])`% for fast pools (95% CI `r sg(tcls$lo[tcls$turnover=="fast"])` to `r sg(tcls$hi[tcls$turnover=="fast"])`, `r tcls$k_obs[tcls$turnover=="fast"]` observations from `r tcls$k_study[tcls$turnover=="fast"]` studies), `r sg(tcls$pct[tcls$turnover=="intermediate"])`% for intermediate pools (95% CI `r sg(tcls$lo[tcls$turnover=="intermediate"])` to `r sg(tcls$hi[tcls$turnover=="intermediate"])`), and `r sg(tcls$pct[tcls$turnover=="slow"])`% for slow pools (95% CI `r sg(tcls$lo[tcls$turnover=="slow"])` to `r sg(tcls$hi[tcls$turnover=="slow"])`).

Two qualifications are necessary. The slow class rests on only `r tcls$k_obs[tcls$turnover=="slow"]` observations from `r tcls$k_study[tcls$turnover=="slow"]` studies, its interval is wide, and its point estimate lies above rather than below the intermediate class, so it does not sit on the fitted line. The ordered result is therefore driven principally by the contrast between fast and intermediate pools, which is well supported, rather than by a demonstrated monotonic decline across all three. Resolving the slow class would require substantially more paired measurements of mineral-associated carbon, and that measurement is the single most valuable addition the field could make to this question.

# Discussion

## 4.1 Rate and stock are not interchangeable

Invasion did not detectably increase soil carbon stocks in this synthesis, while published rate estimates for invaded systems are large and consistently positive. The two findings are not in conflict once it is recognised that they concern different quantities. Stock is the integral of rate over residence time, and a system can accumulate carbon quickly while retaining little.

The mechanism was set out by @peltzer2010effects, who concluded that direct invader effects on forest carbon are smaller and shorter-lived than indirect effects operating through nutrient availability, productivity and species composition, and that these indirect effects govern long-term pools. Rate is measurable within a season and responds immediately to a fast-growing invader. Stock integrates decades of gains and losses and responds only if residence time is preserved. Our fraction results are consistent with residence time falling rather than rising: microbial biomass carbon increased while particulate organic carbon, composed largely of partially decomposed plant residues, decreased, a signature of faster processing rather than accrual. This is supported by evidence that invasion raises nutrient-releasing enzyme activity while leaving carbon-decomposing enzymes inconsistent [@zhou2019enhanced] and increases heterotrophic respiration [@fan2024global].

The turnover test converts this interpretation from a reading of two fractions into a quantitative prediction that the data confirm. Ordering pools by their published turnover time and entering that order as a moderator, the invasion effect declines by `r f1(abs(pct(tord$b[2])))`% per step from fast to slow (*p* `r pf(tord$QMp)`). Invasion therefore does not add carbon uniformly across the soil profile's kinetic classes: it adds carbon to the compartments that turn over fastest and does not add it, and may remove it, from those that persist. Since only the persistent compartments contribute to storage on the timescales relevant to climate mitigation, an increase concentrated in fast pools is consistent with accelerated throughput and inconsistent with accrual. The weakest point in this test is the slow class itself, which is too sparsely measured to resolve, so the inference rests on the fast-to-intermediate contrast rather than on the full ordering.

## 4.2 Two measurement artefacts inflate the apparent stock effect

Two features of how stocks are measured act in the same direction as the rate-stock confusion.

The apparent soil carbon gain existed only in concentration data and vanished among areal stocks. Concentration and stock differ by bulk density, which invasion alters in both directions: it is reduced beneath encroaching woody legumes, where ignoring the change overestimates subcanopy soil carbon by nearly thirty per cent [@throop2008shrub], and the *Spartina* literature notes explicitly that bulk density is often reduced under invasion [@xu2022effects]. The IPCC states the consequence directly, that a fixed-depth stock change can arise entirely from a bulk density change [@ipcc2019refinement], while confining the remedy to higher-tier factor derivation; the 2006 Guidelines, still operative for most inventories, treat bulk density only as a multiplier [@ipcc2006guidelines]. The correction, available for three decades [@ellert1995calculation] and repeatedly shown to matter [@raffeld2024importance; @potash2026empirical], cannot be applied here because no contributing study reported bulk density. That absence is a principal finding: the primary literature is not currently constituted to answer whether invasion changes soil carbon stocks.

Second, the positive response was confined to coastal systems and dominated by one species. This is a rediscovered rather than a novel pattern. The largest published positive result was attributed by its own authors to invaders that "intensify biomass per unit area, extend and elevate coastal wetlands, and convert coastal mudflats into C-rich vegetated habitat" [@davidson2018differential]; where the comparison is against bare tidal flat the difference is very large [@huang2022effects], and where it is against established native marsh it is smaller and expressed as concentration [@wang2018spartina; @xu2022effects]. Sampling conventions compound this: the generic IPCC soil depth default is 30 cm while coastal wetlands are assessed to 1 m [@ipcc2006guidelines; @ipcc2014wetlands], so the systems carrying the positive effect are those conventionally sampled deepest.

## 4.3 The accounting consequence

The IPCC treats the gain-loss and stock-difference methods as equally valid and leaves the choice to expert judgement [@ipcc2006guidelines]. On invaded land that choice determines the answer. A gain-loss assessment, built from increment and loss terms, will register the elevated productivity that invasion reliably produces. A stock-difference assessment, built from inventories separated in time, will register little or nothing, and the guidance itself anticipates this, warning that stock-difference fails where change is small relative to the standing stock.

This matters because carbon crediting pays for durable stock while frequently being justified by rate-like evidence. Projections built on observed growth rates rather than realised stock differences will overstate the credited quantity wherever residence time is shorter than assumed. The direction of error in the land sector is already documented: improved-forest-management baselines have been shown to understate natural accumulation, inflating the credited difference [@west2023action], and an assessment of 182 Australian regeneration projects found changes in credited areas largely mirrored changes in adjacent uncredited land [@macintosh2024australian]. Invasion is a case where rate and stock evidence are both available and disagree, and where the disagreement is mechanistic rather than incidental.

It is worth recording how little accounting frameworks engage with invasion. IPCC carbon pools are defined as physical compartments distinguished by whether material is living or dead, above or below ground, and above or below a size threshold, with no reference to species identity or provenance [@ipcc2006guidelines]. Invasion is consequently invisible to national accounts: an invaded stand and a native stand of equal biomass are indistinguishable, and the guidance supplies default biomass values for species that are aggressive invaders elsewhere. The one peer-reviewed treatment of this gap estimates that invasions of ten problem plants may emit up to 150 Mt CO~2~-equivalent annually in a single country [@mantoani2026invasive].

## 4.4 Bio-perversity

The rate-stock divergence bears directly on a recognised policy risk. @lindenmayer2012avoiding identify three bio-perversities arising from carbon programmes, the second being the planting of trees that become invasive taxa. If carbon programmes reward measured accumulation rates, they will preferentially select fast-growing species, and fast growth is among the traits that predict invasiveness. @pati2025ecological, having found rapid carbon accumulation under *Gliricidia sepium* alongside reduced diversity, conclude that planting invasive species "might create obstruction to achieve the goals of REDD+ and UN resolutions on ecosystem restoration", and title their paper an ecological dilemma.

The contrary case has been argued: that invader biomass should be valorised through established value chains [@nunes2021carbon], or that in degraded systems an invader may build soil carbon more effectively than natives through root-derived inputs to mineral-associated pools [@meitha2024invasive]. Our results do not refute these arguments, which concern particular species in particular settings, but they do bear on the general form of the claim. Where the evidence offered is a rate, it is not evidence about stock, and it is stock that a carbon account records.

## 4.5 What would follow if the divergence is real

Three consequences follow, in ascending order of importance.

For measurement, rate and stock should be reported together. They are currently reported by different subfields using different designs, and a study measuring one has no way of knowing whether the other agrees. @pati2025ecological demonstrate what becomes visible when both are measured on the same plots, and theirs is a rare design rather than a standard one.

For interpretation, evidence of accelerated accumulation should not be presented as evidence of increased storage. This is not a pedantic distinction. In the compiled evidence the two differ by nearly an order of magnitude in the same system, and they differ in sign between compartments in the same study. The literature's apparent disagreement about invasion and carbon substantially dissolves once the quantity being reported is specified.

For policy, the mismatch is systematic rather than incidental. A crediting system that accepts rate-like evidence while issuing credits against stock will over-credit wherever residence time is shorter than assumed, and invasion is a case where there is positive reason to expect exactly that, because the fraction data indicate faster cycling. The direction of this error is the same as that already documented in improved forest management, where baselines understate natural accumulation [@west2023action], and in regeneration projects whose credited areas track adjacent uncredited land [@macintosh2024australian].

The counter-arguments deserve a fair statement. @nunes2021carbon propose valorising invader biomass through established value chains, which is a proposal about the fate of harvested material rather than about standing stock, and is unaffected by our result: material converted to a durable product leaves the land pool and is accounted elsewhere. @meitha2024invasive argue that root-derived carbon from a deep-rooted invader may form mineral-associated soil carbon more efficiently than litter inputs, which is a claim specifically about the durable fraction and is therefore the right kind of claim. Our data cannot test it, because mineral-associated carbon was represented by only `r r_maoc$k_obs` observations from `r r_maoc$k_study` studies. That is the measurement most needed, and its absence is the reason the durability question remains open rather than closed.

## 4.6 Limitations

The two limbs are asymmetric. The stock limb is a formal meta-analysis of `r f0(n_obs)` observations; the rate limb is a compilation of published estimates from four sources, tabulated rather than pooled, and conclusions drawn from it are correspondingly weaker. A formal meta-analysis of rate effects would require paired invaded and uninvaded productivity measurements at a scale that does not currently exist in a deposited form, and assembling it is the obvious next step.

The stock analysis rests on a single deposited compilation and inherits its inclusion criteria and geographical emphasis. Heterogeneity exceeded 99% for every fraction, so pooled estimates describe a distribution rather than a common effect [@senior2016heterogeneity]. The areal subset carrying the central result comprises `r r_area$k` observations from `r n_area_stud` studies. Mineral-associated carbon was too sparsely represented to test. All comparisons are spatial contrasts without pre-invasion measurement, so pre-existing differences influencing where invaders established cannot be excluded, and mechanisms underlying reported impacts are rarely tested directly in this literature [@levine2003mechanisms].

# Conclusions

Biological invasion increases the rate at which carbon is accumulated without reliably increasing the stock that is held. The distinction is not semantic: it corresponds to the two methods the IPCC treats as equally valid, it is visible within single datasets, and it extends beyond plant invaders to effects transmitted through trophic cascades.

Three changes would resolve what remains uncertain. Studies of invasion and carbon should report rates and stocks together, since the divergence is only detectable when both are measured. Soil studies should report bulk density alongside concentration, sample below 30 cm, and express stocks on an equivalent soil mass basis. And carbon accounting for invaded or restored land should state which of the two IPCC methods it applies, because on this land the choice determines the result. Until then, evidence that invasion accelerates carbon accumulation should not be read as evidence that it stores more carbon.

## Data availability

The stock data are openly available from Dryad at doi:10.5061/dryad.c59zw3rkc [@he2025plant]. The compiled rate evidence, the code that tidies the stock data, fits the models and produces every figure and table, and the manuscript source are archived together and require only R and the `metafor` package.
